# What this book establishes {.unnumbered}

This book reports a research program on **surrogates for steady,
boundary-driven, three-dimensional PDE problems**: given a discretized
boundary (a surface mesh with normals and areas) and a few global conditions
such as the freestream direction, predict the fields on that boundary and in
the volume around it. The program built an architecture, ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention; the code class is `ISLA`, formerly `MeshTransformer2`),^[Pronounced "eye-la"; an *isla* is an island, a shape defined entirely by
its boundary. An earlier exact-kernel design of this program is documented in
the repository's `book/archive/` directory, outside this book.] and measured it
against the strongest baseline tested under this protocol, GeoTransolver, under one
frozen, parameter- and token-matched protocol on two production aerodynamics
datasets (DrivAerML, HiLiftAeroML). The
audience is applied mathematicians and machine-learning researchers; every
term is defined at first use and every number is computed live from a
checked-in artifact.

## The verdict {#sec-verdict}

**ISLA has no measured accuracy advantage over GeoTransolver or plain
Transolver once every model receives the freestream at the same unit
scale; the 2.8x small-data advantage this program reported on HiLiftAeroML
was an artifact of the comparison protocol, and what ISLA contributes is a
set of exact contracts that earn a measured 6–19% accuracy lead over
augmented baselines when geometries arrive in arbitrary poses, and an
interior configuration that leads on interior velocity and trails on
pressure and eddy viscosity once the evaluation is scored in float32.** That sentence is the whole book, and every chapter
either supports one clause of it or bounds it.

The artifact, and how it was found. Every surface comparison fed ISLA the
unit freestream direction and fed GeoTransolver and Transolver the physical
freestream velocity, 2679.5 in/s on HiLiftAeroML, because the recipe
nondimensionalizes fields and coordinates but not that global input. An
independent audit noticed the asymmetry and showed that GeoTransolver's
global-context projector, untrained, collapses from about 200 occupied
slices per head at unit magnitude to one slice at the HiLift magnitude
(@sec-part-baseline). The preregistered control retrained both baselines with
the unit direction, changing nothing else. At 35 training cases
GeoTransolver's surface-pressure error fell from 0.381 to 0.124 (0.111 at
its better learning rate) and Transolver's from 0.404 to 0.115; ISLA's is
0.138 (0.123 in the weights-off ablation, a discretization-dependent
configuration this book measures but does not adopt, @sec-principle). Both
baselines are now more accurate than ISLA, on 130 and 152 of the 180
validation cases, by 1.1–1.25x (@sec-de-unit-drive). Every steel-man control run for the baselines
before that (higher learning rate, doubled epochs, a third seed, the same
attention family without a geometry encoder) had kept the input and could not
find it.

What stands, and what waits. On DrivAerML, where GeoTransolver also received
the physical velocity (38.9 m/s), the unit-drive rerun at 435 cars changes
nothing (0.0503 against 0.0498 in float32), and in float32, the reporting
instrument, ISLA is 10% behind the unit-drive GeoTransolver (0.0558 against
0.0503) and 8% behind Transolver (0.0517); below full data GeoTransolver's 1.2–1.3x lead
stands. At 512 width and 80,000 cells the three are within 3% (0.0419 /
0.0428 / 0.0431 in float32), so the full-data deficit is a statement about
the reference size and resolution; there the similarity-gauge ISLA reaches
the same 0.0431 at the same cost while degrading 1.08x under a 10:1
sampling-density bias against 4–17x for every other scaled configuration;
the frame class, not this instance, is what that demonstrates, and the
single reference configuration is the relative-position frame (RELFRAME,
total-measure scale; decided 2026-09-11 with its 11% price at 35 HiLift
cases stated; @sec-nb-frame-full-verdict, @sec-full-data). The fixed-angle
split has been re-measured: the unit-drive GeoTransolver and Transolver
beat ISLA there too (0.029 and 0.032 against 0.036, on 18 of 18 held-out
geometries), so the 5.0x figure is gone as a comparison. The HiLift rungs
above 35 cases have now been re-measured with unit-drive baselines at 210
cases and at 4 and 21 training geometries (@sec-program-status): at 210
cases GeoTransolver is 0.83x of ISLA in float32 (0.053 against 0.064, lower
on 162 of 180 cases) and Transolver 0.91x, at 4 geometries GeoTransolver is
0.76x, at 21 geometries 0.92x; the 2.2x and the unseen-geometry factors were
measurements of a mis-scaled protocol, and the prediction written before the
rerun, that the baselines match or beat ISLA at every rung, has held at
every rung measured (six of seven, the 510-case rung at 0.84x and 0.90x with the baselines lower on 168 of 180 cases; 1,260 cases pending). The regime-extrapolation result stands as it was: across an
angle-of-attack or stall boundary every architecture tested loses about a
factor of ten, so coverage, not architecture, governs that axis.

What ISLA adds is contracts and one configuration. Rotation and translation
covariance are exact by algebraic construction (the finite-precision residual
of the bf16 training path is a measured quantity, @sec-mt2-contracts), and
training is stable across a decade of learning rate where GeoTransolver
degrades 4–14x. On the interior task, with its queries admitted as
interacting tokens and given the signed distance to the wall, ISLA at 8.9M
parameters is 27% more accurate than GeoTransolver's 27.6M-parameter volume
configuration on interior velocity (0.080 against 0.109 in float32), 6% less
accurate on interior pressure (0.055 against 0.052) and 27% less accurate on
eddy viscosity (0.112 against 0.088); the bfloat16 evaluation had inflated
GeoTransolver-volume's errors by 20–23% and ISLA's by 4–7%, which is what
made pressure look like an ISLA lead;
that lead holds only when at least the training count of 10,000 points is
queried together (@sec-interior-companion); it was obtained with about 365
surface tokens rather than the intended 10,000, and a rerun with 10,000
changes nothing (@sec-interior-task); and GeoTransolver-volume also received
the physical velocity, but retrained with the unit direction it changes by
under 2% on every field, so the interior ordering is not an input-scale
artifact (@sec-interior-task). The passive,
query-independent decode is 3.1x behind on pressure as built (float32). Cost: on one
GPU and one instrument ISLA's current code peaks at 1.6 GiB of training
memory against GeoTransolver's 4.1 GiB, the code that trained the checkpoints
peaked at 9.3 GiB, and ISLA's step is 3.7x slower (@sec-cost).

: The standing of ISLA against GeoTransolver in every setting measured, as

## The result in one picture

```{python}
#| label: fig-headline
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The headline and its correction. Surface-pressure relative L2 error on
#|   the shared 180-case HiLiftAeroML validation set versus number of training
#|   cases, for GeoTransolver (red circles), ISLA (blue squares) and plain
#|   Transolver (grey triangles, dashed), as trained under the frozen protocol
#|   in which the baselines received the freestream as a physical velocity
#|   (2679.5 in/s) and ISLA as a unit direction. The open markers at 35 cases
#|   are the same baselines retrained with the unit direction and nothing else
#|   changed: both fall below ISLA. Lines join seed means; bands span the
#|   seeds; the factors are each baseline's error divided by ISLA's (above one
#|   favours ISLA). The higher rungs' unit-drive reruns are training
#|   (@sec-program-status). Protocol: 10,000 sampled surface points per case,
#|   500 epochs, bfloat16, no augmentation, each architecture at its declared
#|   learning rate, three seeds at 35 and 210 cases (two for the unit-drive
#|   arms) and two at 1,260, final-epoch checkpoints, validation set. Data:
#|   results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json,
#|   results/t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json,
#|   results/w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json (third seeds),
#|   results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json (unit-drive arms).
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
BLUE, RED, GREY = "#2a78d6", "#e34948", "#52514e"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})
lad = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json"))
t1 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json"))
w2 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json"))["runs"]
lad = {**lad, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("lad_hl_")}}
t1 = {**t1, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("t1_hl_transolver")}}
rungs = [(35, "lad_hl_{a}_super_scarce_seed{s}"), (210, "lad_hl_{a}_scarce_seed{s}"), (1260, "{a}_hl_lr1_seed{s}")]
data = {}
for arch in ("gt", "mt2"):
    xs, means, lo, hi = [], [], [], []
    for n, pat in rungs:
        v = [lad[pat.format(a=arch, s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43, 44) if pat.format(a=arch, s=s) in lad]
        xs.append(n); means.append(statistics.mean(v)); lo.append(min(v)); hi.append(max(v))
    data[arch] = (xs, means, lo, hi)
xs, means, lo, hi = [], [], [], []
for n, pat in [(35, "t1_hl_transolver_super_scarce_{lr}_seed{s}"), (210, "t1_hl_transolver_scarce_{lr}_seed{s}")]:
    best = None
    for lr in ("lr1e3", "lr3e3"):
        v = [t1[pat.format(lr=lr, s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43, 44) if pat.format(lr=lr, s=s) in t1]
        if len(v) >= 2 and (best is None or statistics.mean(v) < statistics.mean(best)):
            best = v
    xs.append(n); means.append(statistics.mean(best)); lo.append(min(best)); hi.append(max(best))
data["t"] = (xs, means, lo, hi)
udrv = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json"))["arms"]
unit = {"gt": udrv["gt_unit_35"]["seed_pressure"], "t": udrv["transolver_unit_35"]["seed_pressure"]}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 5.2))
style = {"gt": (RED, "GeoTransolver", "o", "-", 2.2), "t": (GREY, "Transolver", "^", "--", 1.6), "mt2": (BLUE, "ISLA", "s", "-", 2.2)}
for arch in ("gt", "t", "mt2"):
    xs, means, lo, hi = data[arch]; c, name, mk, ls, lw = style[arch]
    ax.fill_between(xs, lo, hi, color=c, alpha=0.18, lw=0)
    ax.plot(xs, means, color=c, lw=lw, ls=ls, marker=mk, ms=7, zorder=3, alpha=0.55)
xoff = {"gt": 35 * 0.93, "t": 35 * 1.075}
for arch in ("gt", "t"):
    c, name, mk, ls, lw = style[arch]; v = unit[arch]; m = statistics.mean(v); x = xoff[arch]
    ax.plot([x, x], [min(v), max(v)], color=c, lw=3, alpha=0.5, zorder=4)
    ax.plot([x], [m], marker=mk, ms=10, mfc="white", mec=c, mew=2.2, ls="none", zorder=5)
    ax.annotate("", (x, m), (35, data[arch][1][0]), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=c, lw=1.4, shrinkA=6, shrinkB=8, alpha=0.8))
ax.annotate("GeoTransolver (physical drive)", (35, data["gt"][1][0]), xytext=(22, 16), textcoords="offset points", color=RED, fontweight="bold", va="center",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
ax.annotate("Transolver (physical drive)", (35, data["t"][1][0]), xytext=(22, -4), textcoords="offset points", color=GREY, fontweight="bold", va="center",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
ax.annotate("ISLA", (210, data["mt2"][1][1]), xytext=(14, -14), textcoords="offset points", color=BLUE, fontweight="bold", va="center")
m_gt, m_t = statistics.mean(unit["gt"]), statistics.mean(unit["t"])
ax.annotate(f"unit freestream direction:\nGeoTransolver {m_gt/data['mt2'][1][0]:.2f}x ISLA\nTransolver {m_t/data['mt2'][1][0]:.2f}x ISLA", (35, m_t), xytext=(-8, -30), textcoords="offset points",
            color=INK, fontsize=9, ha="left", va="top", linespacing=1.3, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc="white", ec=BASELINE))
for i, n in enumerate((210,)):
    r_gt = data["gt"][1][1] / data["mt2"][1][1]; r_t = data["t"][1][1] / data["mt2"][1][1]
    ymid = (data["gt"][1][1] * data["mt2"][1][1]) ** 0.5
    ax.text(n * 1.08, ymid, f"physical drive: GeoTransolver {r_gt:.1f}x, Transolver {r_t:.1f}x\nunit-drive rerun training", color=INK2, fontsize=8.5, va="center", linespacing=1.3,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
r_full = data["gt"][1][2] / data["mt2"][1][2]
ax.annotate(f"{r_full:.2f}x (physical drive)", (1260, (data["gt"][1][2] * data["mt2"][1][2]) ** 0.5), xytext=(14, 30), textcoords="offset points", color=INK2, fontsize=9, va="bottom")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xticks([35, 210, 1260]); ax.set_xticklabels(["35", "210", "1,260"])
ax.set_yticks([0.04, 0.06, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4]); ax.set_yticklabels(["0.04", "0.06", "0.10", "0.20", "0.40"]); ax.set_ylim(0.033, 0.6)
ax.set_xlim(22, 3200)
ax.set_xlabel("Training cases [count]", color=INK2)
ax.set_ylabel("Surface pressure error, rel-L2 [–]", color=INK2)
ax.set_title("HiLiftAeroML surface pressure vs training cases: the physical-drive protocol and its unit-drive correction at 35 cases", color=INK, loc="left", fontsize=10, pad=10)
ax.grid(True, which="major", color=GRID); ax.grid(False, which="minor")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## How to read this book

Part I defines the problem, the datasets and splits, the metrics and the
protocol (@sec-problem), then the architecture, ISLA
(@sec-mt2), and the baselines with the fair-comparison rules
(@sec-baselines). Part II is the evidence on production aerodynamics. It
opens with the scoreboard (@sec-scoreboard): every cross-architecture
measurement of the book, surface, interior, pose, consistency and cost, on
one page with matched inputs and one instrument, for a reader who needs the
standing and not the derivation. The chapters behind it are data
efficiency (@sec-data-efficiency); accuracy at full data, the robustness
contracts and regime extrapolation (@sec-full-data,
@sec-regime-extrapolation); and boundary-to-interior prediction
(@sec-interior), which also answers why the architecture does not evaluate
exact boundary-integral kernels (@sec-interior-negatives). Part III
states the limits of every claim and the experiments that would move them
(@sec-limits) and holds the live status ledger of the program
(@sec-program-status). The appendix is the dated lab notebook
(@sec-notebook): every preregistration, launch and verdict, including the
failed ones, in the order they happened.

Three habits of this book: a comparison is only reported when parameters,
tokens per case, epochs, peak memory and the scale of every input are
matched or the mismatch is stated in the same sentence, and every ratio between architectures is written
as baseline error divided by ISLA error, so a value above one favours ISLA; a claim is only reported with the split it was
measured on and the statistic behind it; and a limit is stated next to the
claim it limits, not in a separate place.

## What this book does not claim

It does not claim that ISLA is more accurate than GeoTransolver or plain
Transolver anywhere on the surface task. The HiLiftAeroML figures that once
carried that claim (2.8x at 35 cases, 2.2x at 210, 1.4–1.8x on never-seen
geometries, 5.0x at a fixed angle, 3% force coefficients against 8–17%,
a six-fold data multiplier) were measured against baselines that received
the freestream as a physical velocity of 2,679.5 in/s while ISLA received a
unit direction; with the unit direction the same baselines are 1.1–1.25x more
accurate than ISLA at 35 cases (@sec-de-unit-drive), and the higher rungs are
being re-measured. Those figures appear in this book as measurements of the
physical-drive protocol and as the record of how the artifact was found, not
as comparisons. On DrivAerML GeoTransolver, also fed the physical velocity, is
1.2–1.3x more accurate from 27 cases up. The HiLift accuracy figures are
validation-set figures (final-epoch checkpoints, no checkpoint selection;
the sealed test was spent on regime extrapolation, and because those regime
test sets cover all 180 geometries, every remaining HiLiftAeroML split is
held out per checkpoint but is not an independent program-level
confirmation, @sec-limits-validation). The interior lead is conditional:
it requires at least the training count of points to be queried together,
was obtained with about 365 surface tokens, and awaits the same unit-drive
control for GeoTransolver-volume (@sec-interior). ISLA's exact equivariance is a contract, not an
in-distribution accuracy edge on vehicle data: GeoTransolver trained in a
canonical frame is exactly pose-invariant at 1% cost (@sec-pose). Its
sampling-density robustness belongs to a configuration (the similarity
gauge) that produced no accuracy number in this book
(@sec-robustness-density). Neither architecture generalizes across a
flow-regime boundary, and neither transfers zero-shot to a different vehicle
family (@sec-regime-extrapolation, @sec-full-data).
